payload.title: Closing SAP PM work orders at the asset
payload.metaDescription: Why field crews still close SAP PM work orders on paper, and the three-screen tablet app that changes it without retraining the office.
payload.body:
Most operators who run SAP PM already have the data model they need. The work order, the notification and the equipment record are all there. The problem is where the work order gets closed: on a clipboard in the van, and in SAP on Friday afternoon when someone in the office keys in the week.

## What paper costs you

When a work order is closed days after the job, the details are guessed. Readings are rounded, defects that were noticed but not fixed are forgotten, and the time booked is whatever fits the timesheet. The asset register drifts away from the assets, and preventive maintenance plans start to schedule work that crews know is pointless.

## Three screens, not thirty

Crews do three things with SAP: see today's jobs, close a job with readings and photos, and raise a defect they found on the way. A small Fiori app on a depot tablet can do exactly those three things. It does not need the full transaction, and it should not try to.

Keep the office on the screens they know. Planners and supervisors still schedule, release and settle in the back office. Only the closing moves to the field.

## Roll it out depot by depot

Start with the depot whose supervisor asks for it. Run paper and tablet side by side for a fortnight, then switch. Offline mode matters more than any feature: depots and rural sites often have poor signal, and a tablet that loses the job when the signal drops will be back in the drawer within a week.

## What to measure

Measure the gap between finishing a job and closing it in SAP, and the number of defects raised from the field. Both tell you whether the crews trust the app. Larkwell helps operators plan and build this kind of field app on top of SAP PM.

payload.title: Clearing SAP billing exceptions for good
payload.metaDescription: Billing exceptions in SAP for utilities are a process symptom. Measure them by cause, fix the top two causes, then automate what is left.
payload.body:
Every utility running SAP billing has an exception queue, and most have a team whose job is to work it. When the queue grows, the usual answer is to add people. That clears the backlog for a while and hides the reason it grew.

## Exceptions have causes

Group a month of exceptions by cause before changing anything. In most landscapes a handful of causes account for nearly all of them: meter reads that fail plausibility checks, move-in and move-out dates that cross a billing period, and tariff changes that reached production before anyone tested them against real contracts.

## Fix the process, not the queue

Take the largest cause and trace it back to where the bad data enters. Implausible reads often come from one reading route or one device type. Move-in timing problems usually start in the customer service process, where an agent enters a date the billing run cannot handle. Fix the entry point and that whole class of exception stops arriving.

## Then automate the rest

Once the big causes are fixed, what remains is a smaller, steadier queue. Some of it can be cleared by rules: re-estimate and release, or hold and notify. The rest needs a person, and now that person has time to look properly.

## Test tariffs like code

Tariff changes deserve the same care as a code change: a test system with copies of real contracts, a set of expected bills, and a sign-off before transport. It is slower the first time and much faster after that.

Larkwell works with utilities on billing processes in SAP and on the move to S/4HANA, where these fixes are worth making before the conversion rather than after.

payload.title: Sorting custom code before a brownfield move
payload.metaDescription: Before a brownfield S/4HANA conversion, sort custom code into keep, fix and retire using real usage data from production.
payload.body:
A brownfield conversion keeps your processes and your data, and it also keeps your custom code. That is the point of choosing it, and it is also where most of the surprises come from.

## Start with usage, not with the code

Before anyone reads a line of ABAP, collect usage data from production for a full business cycle, including the year-end close. It tells you which custom programs, reports and enhancements anyone still runs. In older landscapes a large share of custom objects turn out to be unused.

## Three piles

Put every custom object into one of three piles. Retire what nobody uses: delete it before the conversion so nobody has to fix it. Fix what is used and flagged by the conversion checks. Keep and document what is used and passes.

## Fix in the source system

Make the fixes in the current system, transport them through the normal landscape and let them run in production before the conversion. The conversion weekend is the wrong time to find out a fix was wrong.

## Write down why

For every object you keep, write one line on what it does and who asked for it. The next upgrade will be easier, and the team will stop treating custom code as something nobody dares to touch.

Larkwell plans brownfield conversions for operators who cannot stop the depot or the billing run, starting with exactly this kind of inventory.

payload.title: Master data first: the cutover nobody plans
payload.metaDescription: Most failed data loads trace back to master data. Give every object an owner and clean it in the source system before the migration.
payload.body:
Migration plans spend weeks on the load tools and days on the data. Most failed loads trace back to master data: duplicate equipment records, functional locations nobody owns, and business partners with three addresses.

## One owner per object

Equipment, functional locations, materials, business partners: each needs a named owner in the business, not in IT. The owner decides what is a duplicate and what is real.

## Clean in the source

Fix the data in the current system, where people can see and check it. Cleaning in a spreadsheet between extract and load creates a third version of the truth.

## Rehearse the load

Run at least two full rehearsals with production data. Each one finds problems the last one hid.

Larkwell plans data migration as part of every S/4HANA move, starting with master data.

rules.text: Every number (percentage, cost, time saved, statistic) must come from a source we can link to. No source, no number.
No claims about Larkwell results, clients, certifications or awards that aren't verified. Brackenfield Waste and Osterby Utilities are the only clients we may name.
Every piece must tie to one Larkwell service and a real problem that IT and SAP leaders at mid-to-large enterprises are trying to solve. If it doesn't, don't write it.
Don't repeat a theme Larkwell covered in the last two weeks (for example Clean Core or S/4HANA deadline timing). Pick a different service or a genuinely new angle.
Never open a LinkedIn post with the "X often fails" / "is often the difference" / "often leads to" formula. Open with a specific fact, a clear stance or a concrete situation.
Write in UK English: organisation, optimise, modernise, analyse, behaviour.
Don't write about niche regulation or compliance topics (for example EPA e-Manifest or DORA CTPP rules) unless they directly change what an SAP buyer has to do and Larkwell offers help with it.
Sound like a senior SAP practitioner who did the work: plain, specific, calm and honest about trade-offs. No hype, no exclamation marks.
Blog titles are complete phrases of 60 characters or fewer, never cut off mid-phrase.
Be practical about custom code: modernise what earns its keep, retire the rest, and say which is which.
One clear point per LinkedIn post. Cut anything that doesn't support it.
Name the actual SAP thing in every claim (module, transaction, release, migration step). Cut any sentence that could appear in any vendor's post.
Spread across Larkwell's whole service catalogue (Basis, ABAP, plant maintenance, billing, integration, data migration, managed services, Fiori), not just S/4HANA migration.
Open with the point in the first line. No warm-up, no scene-setting, no rhetorical question.
No engagement bait: no questions tacked on just to farm comments, no "Agree?", no fake urgency.
Prefer topics with measured search demand (Search Console queries, the keyword sheet) or a timely SAP announcement, and say which in the reason for writing it.
Blogs answer the search question in the first paragraph and then cover the follow-up questions. Every section adds something new.
Keep fact, opinion and estimate apart. Label an estimate as an estimate.
Match the buyer's stage: problem posts for awareness, cost/approach/comparison pieces for evaluation, Larkwell-specific detail for buyers close to a decision.
Any call to action is soft and specific to the piece (talk to Larkwell about this exact problem), never generic.
No more than one Larkwell LinkedIn post per working day; weekday mornings UK time.

pages.title: S/4HANA migration for operators
pages.summary: Planning an S/4HANA move for a business with depots, crews and meters that cannot stop.
pages.body:
Operators cannot freeze maintenance or billing for a long cutover. What works:

- A readiness check first: custom code, data quality, interfaces. See [[Custom code before a brownfield conversion]].
- Brownfield conversion when the processes are sound; selective when one area (often billing) needs a redesign.
- Cutover planned around the billing run and the maintenance calendar, not the other way round.

Related: [[Utilities billing exceptions]], [[Data migration: master data first]], [[Larkwell Consulting]].

pages.title: SAP Basis managed service
pages.summary: Monitoring, patching and system copies run as a service.
pages.body:
Operators often have one Basis person. A managed service is about cover and routine: a patch window every month with a tested rollback, system copies on a calendar, and alerts that reach someone at night.

Related: [[Larkwell Consulting]], [[Security patch day for operators]].

pages.title: SAP leads at mid-sized utilities
pages.summary: The buyer: practical, short of SAP people, wary of big promises.
pages.body:
They search for a specific problem, read the first paragraph, and leave if it is generic. They trust a named SAP thing (a transaction, a release) more than any adjective.

What they want from content: one useful step they can take this week. See [[Keyword themes 2026]] and [[Utilities billing exceptions]].

pages.title: SAP plant maintenance and field service
pages.summary: Work orders, notifications and preventive plans for crews in the field.
pages.body:
The common failure is not configuration but adoption: crews close work orders on paper and someone keys them in days later. The asset register drifts and preventive plans stop matching reality.

What helps: a small tablet app for the three things crews do (see [[Fiori for field crews]]), notifications raised at the asset, and a monthly review of plans that were skipped.

Proof: [[Case: Brackenfield Waste work orders]]. Search demand: see [[Keyword themes 2026]].

pages.title: Security patch day for operators
pages.summary: A monthly patch window that a small team can keep.
pages.body: Read the notes on the day, rate them against your own landscape, patch development first, and keep a written rollback for each change. See [[SAP Basis managed service]].

pages.title: Utilities billing exceptions
pages.summary: Why billing exceptions pile up in SAP for utilities and how to clear them for good.
pages.body:
Exceptions are a symptom. The usual causes are meter reads that fail validation, move-in and move-out timing, and tariff changes tested too late.

A practical order: measure exceptions by cause for four weeks, fix the top two causes in the process, then automate the rest. Adding people to the exception queue only hides the problem.

Related: [[S/4HANA migration for operators]], [[SAP leads at mid-sized utilities]].

blogs.title: Closing SAP PM work orders at the asset
blogs.metaDescription: Why field crews still close SAP PM work orders on paper, and the three-screen tablet app that changes it without retraining the office.
blogs.body:
Most operators who run SAP PM already have the data model they need. The work order, the notification and the equipment record are all there. The problem is where the work order gets closed: on a clipboard in the van, and in SAP on Friday afternoon when someone in the office keys in the week.

## What paper costs you

When a work order is closed days after the job, the details are guessed. Readings are rounded, defects that were noticed but not fixed are forgotten, and the time booked is whatever fits the timesheet. The asset register drifts away from the assets, and preventive maintenance plans start to schedule work that crews know is pointless.

## Three screens, not thirty

Crews do three things with SAP: see today's jobs, close a job with readings and photos, and raise a defect they found on the way. A small Fiori app on a depot tablet can do exactly those three things. It does not need the full transaction, and it should not try to.

Keep the office on the screens they know. Planners and supervisors still schedule, release and settle in the back office. Only the closing moves to the field.

## Roll it out depot by depot

Start with the depot whose supervisor asks for it. Run paper and tablet side by side for a fortnight, then switch. Offline mode matters more than any feature: depots and rural sites often have poor signal, and a tablet that loses the job when the signal drops will be back in the drawer within a week.

## What to measure

Measure the gap between finishing a job and closing it in SAP, and the number of defects raised from the field. Both tell you whether the crews trust the app. Larkwell helps operators plan and build this kind of field app on top of SAP PM.

blogs.title: Clearing SAP billing exceptions for good
blogs.metaDescription: Billing exceptions in SAP for utilities are a process symptom. Measure them by cause, fix the top two causes, then automate what is left.
blogs.body:
Every utility running SAP billing has an exception queue, and most have a team whose job is to work it. When the queue grows, the usual answer is to add people. That clears the backlog for a while and hides the reason it grew.

## Exceptions have causes

Group a month of exceptions by cause before changing anything. In most landscapes a handful of causes account for nearly all of them: meter reads that fail plausibility checks, move-in and move-out dates that cross a billing period, and tariff changes that reached production before anyone tested them against real contracts.

## Fix the process, not the queue

Take the largest cause and trace it back to where the bad data enters. Implausible reads often come from one reading route or one device type. Move-in timing problems usually start in the customer service process, where an agent enters a date the billing run cannot handle. Fix the entry point and that whole class of exception stops arriving.

## Then automate the rest

Once the big causes are fixed, what remains is a smaller, steadier queue. Some of it can be cleared by rules: re-estimate and release, or hold and notify. The rest needs a person, and now that person has time to look properly.

## Test tariffs like code

Tariff changes deserve the same care as a code change: a test system with copies of real contracts, a set of expected bills, and a sign-off before transport. It is slower the first time and much faster after that.

Larkwell works with utilities on billing processes in SAP and on the move to S/4HANA, where these fixes are worth making before the conversion rather than after.

blogs.title: Sorting custom code before a brownfield move
blogs.metaDescription: Before a brownfield S/4HANA conversion, sort custom code into keep, fix and retire using real usage data from production.
blogs.body:
A brownfield conversion keeps your processes and your data, and it also keeps your custom code. That is the point of choosing it, and it is also where most of the surprises come from.

## Start with usage, not with the code

Before anyone reads a line of ABAP, collect usage data from production for a full business cycle, including the year-end close. It tells you which custom programs, reports and enhancements anyone still runs. In older landscapes a large share of custom objects turn out to be unused.

## Three piles

Put every custom object into one of three piles. Retire what nobody uses: delete it before the conversion so nobody has to fix it. Fix what is used and flagged by the conversion checks. Keep and document what is used and passes.

## Fix in the source system

Make the fixes in the current system, transport them through the normal landscape and let them run in production before the conversion. The conversion weekend is the wrong time to find out a fix was wrong.

## Write down why

For every object you keep, write one line on what it does and who asked for it. The next upgrade will be easier, and the team will stop treating custom code as something nobody dares to touch.

Larkwell plans brownfield conversions for operators who cannot stop the depot or the billing run, starting with exactly this kind of inventory.

blogs.title: A patch window a small Basis team can keep
blogs.metaDescription: A monthly SAP patch routine for a Basis team of one or two people: rate, patch development first, and keep a written rollback.
blogs.body:
Small Basis teams rarely skip patching on purpose. It slips because the patch window competes with everything else, and nobody owns the decision of what to patch first.

## Rate notes against your own landscape

Read the security notes on the day they come out and rate each one against what you actually run. A critical note for a component you do not use is not urgent for you.

## Development first, always

Patch development, let it run for a few days, then quality, then production. Write the rollback for each change before you start.

## Put it in the calendar

A fixed monthly window agreed with the business is easier to keep than an ad hoc one. If the team is one person, a managed service can cover the routine and the nights.

blogs.metaDescription: Most failed data loads trace back to master data. Give every object an owner and clean it in the source system before the migration.
blogs.body:
Migration plans spend weeks on the load tools and days on the data. Most failed loads trace back to master data: duplicate equipment records, functional locations nobody owns, and business partners with three addresses.

## One owner per object

Equipment, functional locations, materials, business partners: each needs a named owner in the business, not in IT. The owner decides what is a duplicate and what is real.

## Clean in the source

Fix the data in the current system, where people can see and check it. Cleaning in a spreadsheet between extract and load creates a third version of the truth.

## Rehearse the load

Run at least two full rehearsals with production data. Each one finds problems the last one hid.

Larkwell plans data migration as part of every S/4HANA move, starting with master data.
